concept.body: Two pair types when lines cross: a LINEAR pair sits on a straight line and SUMS to 180° (supplementary); a VERTICAL pair sits opposite the crossing and is EQUAL. Adjacent → add to 180; opposite → equal. Match the picture before you compute.

explanationVariants: Vertical (opposite) angles are equal, so the partner of a 68° angle is 68°.
Opposite the crossing means equal — 68° maps to 68°.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle is 68°. What is its VERTICAL (opposite) angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 112° = 180 − 68 is the LINEAR-pair neighbor (adjacent, on the straight line). The VERTICAL angle is EQUAL: 68°.
22° = 90 − 68 is the complement — not a crossing-lines relationship. Vertical angles are equal: 68°.

steps.body: Your first real theorem — one you already believe: **vertical angles are equal.** When two lines cross, the opposite angles match. You've used this since Grade 7; now you'll see WHY it can't fail. The engine is the **linear pair**: two angles on a straight line always sum to 180°.

widget.prompt: One angle of a linear pair is fixed at 50°. Drag the other angle until the pair completes a straight line.
widget.successFeedback: 130°, since 50 + 130 = 180. A linear pair always fills a straight angle — that is what the name means — so knowing one angle hands you the other by subtraction, every time.
widget.lowFeedback: Not there yet — the two angles do not yet total 180°.
widget.highFeedback: Past 130° — the pair now totals more than a straight line.

explanationVariants: A linear pair's two angles together form a STRAIGHT angle, which measures 180° by definition — so they're supplementary.
The outer rays of a linear pair point in opposite directions along one line: a straight angle, 180°.

widget.prompt: Why does a linear pair of angles always sum to 180°?

options.label: Together they form a straight angle, which is 180°
options.feedback: The two angles fill a straight line exactly — a straight angle — so their measures total 180°.

options.label: Because all angles sum to 180°
options.feedback: Only pairs forming a straight line sum to 180° — not every angle pair does. A linear pair is exactly the straight-line case.

options.label: Because the two angles are always equal
options.feedback: A linear pair is equal only when both are 90°. In general they're unequal but still SUM to 180°.

options.label: Because vertical angles are equal
options.feedback: That's the theorem we're trying to PROVE — a linear pair's 180° comes from the straight angle, and is what we'll USE to prove it.

steps.body: Here's the whole argument in one breath. Two lines cross, making angle **1** next to angle **2**, and angle **2** next to angle **3**. Then ∠1 + ∠2 = 180° and ∠2 + ∠3 = 180° (two linear pairs). Both equal 180°, so ∠1 + ∠2 = ∠2 + ∠3 — subtract ∠2 and **∠1 = ∠3**. The vertical angles are equal.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross, forming ∠1 and ∠3 vertical, with ∠2 adjacent to each. Order the proof that ∠1 = ∠3.

misorderFeedback.feedback: You can't set the two sums equal before you've WRITTEN both linear-pair equations — establish each 180° first.
Subtracting ∠2 only works once ∠1 + ∠2 = ∠2 + ∠3 is on the page — that equation comes first.

widget.missFeedback: Two linear pairs (each 180°), set the sums equal, subtract the shared ∠2 — then conclude.
widget.successFeedback: Two linear pairs → equal sums → subtract ∠2 → ∠1 = ∠3. That's the proof.

steps.body: Which step does the real work?
explanationVariants: Subtracting the shared ∠2 from both equal sums is the key move — it isolates ∠1 = ∠3.
Both linear pairs equal 180°, so their sums are equal; cancelling the common ∠2 leaves the vertical angles equal.

widget.prompt: In the vertical-angles proof, what single move turns the two linear-pair equations into ∠1 = ∠3?

options.label: Subtracting the shared angle ∠2 from both equal sums
options.feedback: Both sums equal 180° (hence each other); removing the common ∠2 leaves ∠1 = ∠3.

options.label: Measuring ∠1 and ∠3 with a protractor
options.feedback: Measuring gives one example, not a proof. The algebra of subtracting ∠2 settles all cases at once.

options.label: Assuming ∠1 = ∠3 to begin with
options.feedback: Assuming the conclusion is circular. The proof DERIVES it by cancelling ∠2, never assumes it.

options.label: Adding the two equations together
options.feedback: Adding gives ∠1 + 2∠2 + ∠3 = 360 — a tangle. SUBTRACTING the shared ∠2 is the clean move.

explanationVariants: Vertical angles are equal, so 3x + 10 = 5x − 30 → 40 = 2x → x = 20.
Set the two vertical-angle expressions equal and solve: x = 20.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle measures (3x + 10)°; its VERTICAL angle measures (5x − 30)°. Solve for x.

commonErrors.feedback: x = 25 comes from treating them as a LINEAR pair: (3x+10)+(5x−30)=180. But VERTICAL angles are EQUAL, so set 3x+10 = 5x−30 → x = 20.
x = 10 solves 3x + 10 = 5x − 30 only if you slip a sign — recheck: 10 + 30 = 5x − 3x gives 40 = 2x, so x = 20.

hints: The (4x)° angle and the (2x + 30)° angle sit on a straight line — what's their sum?
Solve 6x + 30 = 180 for x, then the vertical angle of the 4x angle equals 4x.
explanationVariants: The two given angles are a linear pair: 4x + (2x + 30) = 180 → 6x = 150 → x = 25. The 4x angle is 100°, and its VERTICAL angle equals it: 100°.
Solve the linear pair for x = 25, so 4x = 100°; vertical angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 100°.

widget.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle is (4x)° and the angle NEXT to it (a linear pair) is (2x + 30)°. Find the measure of the angle VERTICAL to the (4x)° angle, in degrees.

commonErrors.feedback: 80° is the (2x + 30) angle at x = 25 — the LINEAR-pair neighbor. The angle VERTICAL to 4x equals 4x itself: 4(25) = 100°.
25 is the value of x, not an angle. Substitute: the 4x angle is 100°, and its vertical angle equals it: 100°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Linear pair: 6x + 30 = 180 → x = 25; the 4x angle is 100°, and its vertical angle equals it: 100°.

takeaways: Linear pair: two angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
Two linear pairs share an angle; cancelling it proves the vertical angles equal.
Now you can USE ∠1 = ∠3 with confidence — and with algebra.
